meta.description: Research interests and projects by Abdullah Al Bashit

projects.title: Donor and Treatment Choice in Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation
description: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation replaces a patient's blood-forming system with stem cells from a donor, and it can cure acute myeloid leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia and myelodysplastic syndromes. The donor's immune cells attack the remaining cancer, but they can also attack the patient's own tissues. Apart from relapse, this complication, graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), causes the most deaths after transplant. Clinicians lower the risk by choosing a donor whose human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genes match the patient's, because immune cells use HLA proteins to tell self from non-self. Clinicians also choose the graft, the conditioning treatment given before transplant and the drugs that prevent GvHD. Donor selection guidelines rank donors mainly by HLA match and donor age, so they give no estimate of how a given patient will fare with a given donor and treatment.

In MATCH (Artificial Intelligence for Donor Matching), an ARPA-H project with the NMDP, we build models that estimate a patient's outcomes under the available donor and treatment options before transplant. The models learn from records of past transplants in the registry of the Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research (CIBMTR). The records include allele-level HLA typing of patients and donors along with age, disease, comorbidity, graft source, conditioning and GvHD prophylaxis. From the records, a deep time-to-event network estimates the risk of acute GvHD by day 100 and of chronic GvHD, relapse and death by one year, and it updates the risks as events occur after transplant. We also bound the accuracy that the recorded variables allow, which separates the limits of the data from the limits of the models. To compare treatments, we estimate the effects of post-transplant cyclophosphamide, a chemotherapy drug given after transplant to prevent GvHD, and of bone marrow against peripheral blood stem cells as the graft. We check both effects against randomized trials of the two choices. We aim to give clinicians a tool that compares a patient's likely outcomes across donors and treatments when they plan a transplant.

projects.title: Aging Pathway Curation for Multi-omic Assays
description: Drugs that slow aging take many years to test, because a trial must wait for differences in age-related disease or death. Biomarkers that respond to a drug within months could shorten such trials, but randomized trials have tested few candidates. Completed clinical trials allow that test, because their stored blood samples come from people randomized to a drug or a placebo. FAST (Finding Aging Biomarkers by Searching Existing Trials), an ARPA-H project led by Columbia University, measures stored samples from completed trials on six assay platforms, which cover proteins, metabolites and DNA methylation.

To interpret the measurements as aging biology, we curate aging pathways from multi-omic evidence. The evidence comes from the Human Aging Atlas, a public reference that gathers genomic, epigenetic, transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic associations with aging from six independent published sources. The Atlas records the source and evidence type of the associations, because an association in one layer, such as a CpG site whose methylation changes with age, does not establish evidence in another layer. From this evidence, we select the Reactome pathways that draw support from at least two independent sources, so that no single dataset decides which pathways count as aging pathways. We then link the analytes on the six FAST platforms to the aging pathways through standard identifiers (UniProt for proteins, ChEBI for metabolites and the nearby gene for CpG probes). Analytes that cannot be linked keep a flag with the reason, so no analyte goes unaccounted for. The links connect a drug's effect on a protein, metabolite or CpG site in the trial samples to an aging pathway.

projects.title: Structural Characterization of Pathological Inclusions in Alzheimer's Disease
description: In Alzheimer's disease, the proteins amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau aggregate into fibrils that accumulate in brain tissue. Antibodies that clear amyloid plaques now slow cognitive decline in early disease, but researchers do not yet know how the fibrils form and change as the disease advances. Fibril structure may hold part of the answer, because one protein can fold into more than one fibril form, and the forms may damage tissue differently. Current methods cannot measure fibril structure where the fibrils sit. PET and MRI image the whole brain, but at a resolution far too coarse for fibril structure. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and solid-state NMR resolve fibrils in atomic detail, but only after the fibrils are purified from tissue, so the measurement loses the position of a fibril in the brain.

Scanning X-ray microdiffraction keeps that position, because it measures fibril structure inside thin sections of tissue. A synchrotron X-ray beam a few micrometers wide steps across the section and records a diffraction pattern at successive positions, so the patterns form a map of the section. Recovering fibril structure from the patterns poses an inverse problem with a weak signal, because the surrounding tissue scatters far more strongly than the fibrils and the detector adds noise. With neuropathologists at Massachusetts General Hospital and biophysicists at Brookhaven National Laboratory, we develop statistical signal processing and machine learning methods that separate the fibril signal from the tissue background and classify the patterns as Aβ, tau or tissue. We compare the fibril signal with diffraction patterns calculated from cryo-EM and solid-state NMR structures, and we map protein accumulation and tissue loss across disease stages. We aim to identify which fibril forms appear as tissue degenerates, so that future treatments could target those forms.

projects.title: Multi-omic Risk Stratification in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) narrows the airways and destroys the walls of the air sacs (emphysema), and it ranks among the leading causes of death worldwide. Treatment options have grown over the past decade and now include biologic drugs and valves placed in the airways to reduce lung volume. Clinicians still choose among the options with coarse measures, such as a spirometry value that summarizes lung function in one number and a CT score of total emphysema. Such measures describe the lung as a whole, so they show neither the failing lung region nor the biological process behind the damage.

We link molecular measurements in blood to damage in specific regions of the lung, so that a blood test can point to both the process and the region. The data come from the COPDGene study, which follows a large cohort of current and former smokers for about ten years with chest CT, spirometry, blood RNA sequencing and plasma proteomics. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) groups genes and proteins into modules of co-expressed molecules, and canonical correlation analysis (CCA) relates the modules to emphysema in lung regions defined on CT. A high-dimensional causal mediation model then tests which plasma proteins carry the effect of smoking on emphysema progression. We develop a multi-omic risk score from the proteins this model selects, as a weighted sum of protein levels from a routine blood draw. We design the score to rank patients by risk of lung-function decline, emphysema progression, exacerbations and death. The proteins in the score should also indicate the lung regions and pathways behind that risk, so that treatment could begin before the disease destroys more lung tissue.
